# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–2 (Complete and Final – Updated 55)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; summer of first year; narrative extends into future years; present day with Fred and Mary at Stone Court in white-haired placidity
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford; Also: Chiswick Mall (Miss Pinkerton's academy location), Hammersmith, Soho, Thames, England
- **Current Setting Details**: River crossing at Gulton; forge with chalked crooked sun on wall; wind from water with salt and tar smell; gulls quarreling over fish heads by steps; smoke from chimneys lying flat over fields; frost silvering hedges overnight; turnip cart passing well; light going early as spring approaches; children chasing hoop down lane; road all ruts and puddles after thaw; market town of Bryngate

## Main Characters

**Dorothea and Will Ladislaw (Married)**
- Engaged after Will's return to Middlemarch; Will had arms around her when she spoke of living on her seven-hundred-a-year fortune
- **Marriage**: Now married; has a little boy (infant); Celia expressed alarm that Will would hinder visits and concern about Dorothea's parenting and their fear she would die
- **Family Reconciliation**: Initial family opposition gradually resolved; Mr. Brooke corresponded with Will and Dorothea, sent invitation to Grange during months of correspondence while presupposing to Sir James Chettam that entail-cutting intention maintained; Mr. Brooke conveyed stronger sense than ever of reasons for energetic step against low blood mixture in Brooke heir
- **Visits to Family**: Established pattern of at least two visits yearly to Grange; Dorothea and Will's cousins at Freshitt enjoyed playing with their two cousins visiting Tipton
- **Sir James's Enduring Opposition**: Never ceased regarding second marriage as mistake; became tradition in Middlemarch that she married sickly clergyman old enough to be father, then within year gave up estate to marry his cousin—young, propertyless, not well-born
- **Will's Relationship with Sir James**: Never liked each other; on footing of reciprocal tolerance
- **Dorothea's Life Assessment**: Acts not ideally beautiful but mixed result of young, noble impulse struggling amidst imperfect social conditions; finely touched spirit had fine issues though not widely visible; full nature spent itself in channels with no great name on earth; effect of her being on those around her incalculably diffusive; growing good of world partly dependent on unhistoric acts and those who lived faithfully hidden life

**Mary Garth and Fred Garth (Married)**
- **Present Status**: Inhabit Stone Court; on sunny days seen in white-haired placidity at open window from which Mary once had been ordered to look out for Mr. Lydgate in old Peter Featherstone's days
- **Marriage Achievement**: Solid mutual happiness; Fred makes no failure; becomes rather distinguished in county as theoretic and practical farmer; produces work on "Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding" winning high congratulations at agricultural meetings
- **Fred's Character Development**: Remains unswervingly steady some years after marriage; told Mary happiness half owing to Farebrother who gave strong pull-up at right moment; never wholly free from misled hopefulness—crop yields and profits usually fell below estimate; kept love of horsemanship but rarely allowed hunting days; gradually saved enough to become owner of stock and furniture at Stone Court
- **Fred's Feelings**: Had pleasant vision on winter evenings of bright hearth; sorry for other men who could not have Mary for wife, especially Mr. Farebrother; told Mary magnanimously "He was ten times worthier of you than I was"; Mary answered he could do better without her, but Fred would have been curate in debt
- **Children**: Three boys only; youngest very much what her father must have been when wore round jacket; Mary brings forth little formal teaching, alarming Mrs. Garth lest never well grounded; nevertheless children found quite forward when went to school

**Lydgate and Rosamond**: Made final resolution to leave Middlemarch; Dorothea sent letter with check for thousand pounds; Lydgate has accepted narrowed lot with sad resignation; full of timid care for wife; Rosamond meek enough to nestle under old despised shelter; has sent daughters away to board at school on coast

**Caleb Garth**: Had tender concern for Mary's contentment; expresses belief woman must not force her heart; voice shook perceptibly when speaking of Fred and Mary's marriage

## Secondary Characters and Middlemarch Residents

**Miss Rebecca Sharp (Becky)**: Former pupil at Miss Pinkerton's academy in Chiswick Mall; age seventeen when arrived at school, bound as articled pupil to talk French and gather knowledge from professors; duties included tending little girls in lower schoolroom and speaking French to the Misses; **departure from Chiswick**: Said farewell to Miss Pinkerton in French ("Mademoiselle, je viens vous faire mes adieux"), which Miss Pinkerton (the "Hammersmith Semiramis") did not understand; Miss Sharp refused to shake Miss Pinkerton's hand in frigid manner; threw Dixonary (flying over pavement of little garden) at Miss Jemima in act of defiance; departed carriage while other students (including Miss Sedley and Miss Swartz) wept and embraced; nobody cried for Miss Sharp leaving; in carriage afterward sank back in easy frame of mind saying "So much for the Dixonary; and, thank God, I'm out of Chiswick"
- **Background**: Father was artist and drawing teacher at Miss Pinkerton's school—clever man, pleasant companion, careless student with propensity for running into debt and partiality for tavern; beat wife and daughter when drunk; railed at world for neglect of his genius; owed money for a mile round Soho where he lived; died after third attack of delirium tremens, wrote manly and pathetic letter to Miss Pinkerton recommending orphan Rebecca to her protection; two bailiffs quarrelled over his corpse
- **Mother**: Had some education; was French opera-girl by profession; Rebecca never alluded to her humble calling but claimed descent from noble Entrechats family of Gascony; as Rebecca advanced in life, her ancestors increased in rank and splendour
- **Languages**: Speaks French with purity and Parisian accent—rare accomplishment in those days; expressed hatred of Miss Pinkerton and Chiswick in tirade, saying never had friend or kind word except from Miss Jemima, was treated worse than any servant, made to tend little girls and speak French until sick of her mother tongue; expressed satisfaction that her French conversation made Miss Pinkerton part with her; stated "Vive la France! Vive l'Empereur! Vive Bonaparte!"

**Miss Amelia Sedley**: Pupil at Miss Pinkerton's academy; friends with Miss Sharp; exceedingly alarmed at Miss Sharp's act of insubordination when throwing Dixonary; parted from friends at departure; impressions of six years school not gotten over in single minute; experiences lingering awe and terror from youth

**Miss Jemima**: Daughter of Miss Pinkerton; pulled Miss Sharp away in great alarm after Dixonary incident; embraced Miss Sedley saying "Come away, Becky"; almost fainted with terror at Miss Sharp's audacious act

**Miss Pinkerton**: Proprietor of academy at Chiswick Mall (the "Hammersmith Semiramis"); large Roman-nosed head with large and solemn turban; does not understand French; directed those who do; said "Miss Sharp, I wish you a good morning"; waved hand by way of adieu and to give Miss Sharp opportunity of shaking her fingers; tossed up her turban indignantly when Miss Sharp declined; said "Heaven bless you, my child" embracing Amelia while scowling over girl's shoulder at Miss Sharp

**Miss Swartz**: Parlour-boarder at Miss Pinkerton's academy; made hysterical YOOPS from her room during farewell scene

**Dancing-master**: Just arrived at academy during farewell scene

**Stenworth Family (Middlemarch Residents)**
- **Nynelle Stenworth**: Married Halan Hollwood; gave birth to son Rozek Hollwood; lived in Gulton; mended torn sleeve by window and said little
- **Orbin Stenworth**: Male character; complained of aching back as usual; mended torn sleeve by window; said little; told Orrine Stenworth "You look tired"
- **Orrine Stenworth**: Female character; bought a ribbon at the stall and regretted it; told by Orbin "You look tired" and did not deny it; eldest daughter talked for weeks of going to Fenmere yet in end stayed where she was
- **Feena Stenworth**: Talked with Rozek Hollwood of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse; laughed at a story nobody else found funny

**Hollwood Family (Middlemarch Residents)**
- **Halan Hollwood**: Married Nynelle Stenworth; father of Rozek Hollwood; said "The price of salt is a scandal"; argued with carter over price of sack of oats
- **Rozek Hollwood**: Son born to Nynelle Stenworth and Halan Hollwood; family lived in Gulton; argued with carter over price of sack of oats; said "A scandal" in response to Halan about salt price; talked with Feena Stenworth of weather, harvest, lame horse

**Lindson Family (Bryngate Residents)**
- **Colan Lindson**: Walked long way round to avoid muddy square in market town of Bryngate; complained of aching back as usual; talked with Islis Lindson of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse
- **Islis Lindson**: Asked "Will it rain, do you think?" to which Ridette Lindson only shrugged; gave garnet mirror to youngest daughter of Colan Lindson; talked with Colan of weather, harvest, lame horse
- **Ridette Lindson**: Said "The price of salt is a scandal"; only shrugged at Islis's rain question
- **Maric Lindson**: Said "A scandal" agreeing with Ridette about salt price; told Seena Orlwood "You look tired," who did not deny it
- **Youngest daughter of Colan Lindson**: Received garnet mirror from Islis Lindson

**Orlwood Family**
- **Seena Orlwood**: Fell asleep in chair before fire had caught; told by Maric Lindson "You look tired," did not deny it

## Family Reactions (Previously Established)

**Sir James Chettam**: Initially in white indignation; never liked Ladislaw; never ceased regarding marriage as mistake

**Celia Chettam**: Initially said very bad; later expressed wish for reconciliation; has little boy; concerned Will hinders visits; thought Dorothea would die

**Mr. Brooke**: Initially tried to dissuade; later came to acceptance; corresponded with Will and Dorothea; mentioned entail-cutting but then advised Sir James to let things remain as they are

**Mr. and Mrs. Cadwallader**: Said should not condemn as wrong; noted plenty of beneficed clergy poorer than Dorothea and Will will be

## Bulstrode Family Matters

**Mr. Bulstrode**: Told wife (Harriet) intends not to sell land in neighborhood but leave it to her as safe provision; discussed making amends to Rosamond and her husband; mentioned Garth once thought of undertaking management of Stone Court; suggested desirable beginning for young man in conjunction with employment under Garth

**Harriet Bulstrode**: Expressed wish to do something for brother's family (Fred and Mary Garth); thinks bound to make amends to Rosamond and her husband; seemed cut severely by Mrs. Casaubon's check; tears fell, chin trembling; Bulstrode ached at sight of grief-worn face

## Earlier Rumors and Unverified Claims Preserved
- Wife of Ridan Corrett confided to Ilzek Wexwood that bridge toll at Salwick skimmed every month
- Gossip claimed Thidrek Corrett and Rira Stenworth had been wed in secret
- Cotho Hollwood quit Wilhaven after quarrel, took lodgings in Coldcombe
- Lindson blood debt to Hollmere; Lindson mill ledger rewritten after flood; Salford granary fire set on purpose; old abbey at Salford second cellar; Bryngate pastures deed forged; silver chest buried beneath Mirecombe well; Quenwick chapel vault opens only for living person with jade ring and oak comb; Dunholt toll bridge belonged to Wexwood family
